body_markdown:
Transmissions can make or break a car. Not just when they fail, but when they fail to inspire on a test drive. Or even before the test drive, if they lack the right specifications for potential owners. Manuals are the best example, as there was a time when a better shifter, optimized ratios, or an extra gear could determine a sale. That’s a trivial concern these days, as it feels like we have enough gears for everyone to cheer about. Or maybe it’s for everyone to jeer?


There’s no doubt that a gearbox with more than seven gears makes a vehicle perform significantly differently than something with 4 or 5 gears. But the extra cogs come at a price, especially certain 10-speed automatics in certain applications. I am not naming names, because I wanted to ask the Hagerty Media staff a similar question:


*How many (forward) gears are too many in a transmission, and why do you feel that way?*


## Six of One, Half a Dozen the Other


Chevrolet


“I think any more than six gears is nuts, be it automatic or manual. Among the few exceptions to the rule are ZF eight-speed (8HP70, 8HP76, 8HP90) automatics. If you need more gears than that, you need more low-end torque to spin a wider-ratio transmission.


Also, it seems like automatic transmissions get seriously garbage-y after six gears, especially after their warranty expires. Maybe I’d be a bigger fan of modern automatics if automakers would admit they need fluid services every 50,000 miles or so. Vehicles would have a longer service life, customers will save money, rebuilds will likely be cheaper, and shopping for a reliable used car would be less of a minefield.” — *Sajeev Mehta*


## Unlucky Sevens


Hagerty Marketplace | TorchRedZ51


“In a manual? Seven is too many. That’s not based in logic; it’s just one H too many for me. For automatics, I never had a problem with a good ol’ four-speed, but I’ve been in a few eight-speed autos that did a good job always being in the right gear and not hunting.


But you’re right, Sajeev, mo’ complexity usually means mo’ problems.” — *Eddy Eckart*


“I kinda like the seven-speed on the Corvette, Eddy. Without that seventh gear, reverse is just hanging out all alone.” — *Brandan Gillogly*


## Don’t Touch With a 10-foot Pole


“I think that Ford and Chevy have shown us that 10 gears on an automatic are way too many. An eight-gear ‘box was pushing the limits already. In the hunt for efficiency, we’ve surpassed the limits of what is mechanically possible to accomplish in the packaging constraints of a light-duty vehicle’s gearbox, leading to major reliability issues.


For a manual, I’m with Eddy; seven is just a weird number, and I don’t like it on that basis alone.” — *Greg Ingold*


## Deep-Sixed


Marin-Tomas via Getty Images


“If the goal is fuel economy, then there is no limit to the number of gears that makes sense (looking at you, CVT). If the goal is performance, then six seems a natural limit, particularly for a manual.


Any more and the UX is too complicated; you get ‘lost in transmission.’ Does Porsche really need two overdrives to make a 911 work as intended? Ditto if you’re slapping paddles to manually shift an automatic, there is no joy in working a trans with more than six ratios. Computers can easily keep track of more ratios, and a 10-speed can be calibrated to be seamless and transparent, but the magic is in the calibrations.” — *Aaron Robinson*


## It’s All Gravy


Chevrolet


“In manuals *(and I don’t mean paddle shifters—ever!)* six is good, seven just seems wrong. In automatics, I don’t care. I’ve been entertained by some Ford 10-speeds, but since I have never understood how an automatic transmission works *(and never will, so don’t try to explain it)* , I’m easily impressed.


I actually liked the Powerglide, and still do on a drag strip, so anything over two is gravy.”— *Steven Cole Smith*


## Truck, Yeah!


Stefan Lombard


“I drove a 10-speed manual in my trucking days, with five low gears and a splitter that gave you five high gears, all of which were necessary to get 60,000 pounds under way and then keep it under way. It was perfect. Is a 10-speed automatic really necessary in a light-duty pickup truck?


The goal there skews more toward efficiency than moving big loads, but it seems the gremlins inherent in so many of today’s complicated 10-speeds outweigh any benefits over the life of a truck. I’d argue five or six is the sweet spot.” — *Stefan Lombard*
